He conducted us into a large room, furnished with great comfort
and even luxury, but with an air of neglect about it.

Hatherley Farm was a comfortable-looking place, with a garden
stocked with flowers and a wide, well-kept lawn. A large
honey-coloured dog lay sprawled in the sunshine before the door.
A maid-servant answered our knock, and, having satisfied herself
that our visit was professional, she admitted us without further
question. A tall, gaunt man with a severe face and a slight
sandy moustache met us at the door of the sitting-room. He
introduced himself as Mr. Turner.  His face was drawn and his
manner was weary and languid.

A long, rambling, whitewashed house, with a porch and many out-
buildings, stood back from the road. Behind it were fields, and
beyond the fields the dark, irregular line of the distant woods.
As we drove up a gentleman dressed in grey came out to meet us.
This was Mr. Turner, who had recovered somewhat from his illness
but still looked pale and weak. He greeted Lestrade and Holmes
with a courtesy which was almost deferential.

"It is most kind of you to come out here personally," said he.
"But, of course, it is a case of great importance, and if you can
throw any light on it I should be most thankful. The local
police, though they have done all that is possible, have
concluded that there is nothing more which can be done."

"We hope to make some progress," Holmes answered. "We would
like to see the ground where the tragedy occurred. And then, I
think, we shall have some questions to ask of you."

Hatherley Farm was a comfortable-looking place, standing low among
the trees, with a considerable garden, and a carriage-drive
sweeping round to the front door. A gentleman in a grey suit, who
we afterwards learned was the lodge-keeper, was waiting for us
upon the lawn. Holmes exchanged a few words with him, and then,
followed by Lestrade and myself, he walked swiftly across the
garden. The lawn ended at a sharply defined line of wood, which
grew down to the edge of a small lake. This was the Boscombe Pool,
surrounded by the dense shrubbery.

"Yes, that is it." It was a widespread, comfortable-looking
building, two-storied, slate-roofed, with great yellow blotches
of lichen upon the grey walls. The drawn blinds and the smokeless
chimneys, however, gave it a stricken look, as though the weight
of this horror still lay heavy upon it. We called at the door,
when the maid, at Holmes' request, showed us the boots which her
master wore at the time of his death, and also a pair of the
son's, though not the pair which he had then had. Having measured
these very carefully from seven or eight different points, Holmes
desired to be led to the court-yard, from which we all followed
the winding track which led to Boscombe Pool.

At the edge of the pool there was a narrow fringe of grass, and
then a steep drop down to the water itself. Here the wet mud
was marbled with the numerous footprints of those who had
previously visited the scene. Holmes examined the muddy edges
carefully, and then, with a sudden sharp exclamation, pointed
down to the gravel of the path. "Here is something which may help
us," he cried, stooping down to look more closely at a print.
"What is it?" I asked.

"It appears to be a woman's shoe-mark," he said, peering at it.
"At least, it is far smaller than any of the others. No, there
are two of them. Here is another exactly similar."

"What do you make of that?" asked Lestrade, glancing impatiently
at his watch.

"I make this of it," said Holmes, "that there is a woman in the
case. This is really very interesting."

"Interesting?" exclaimed Lestrade, "what is interesting in a
woman's shoe-mark?"

At last he stopped, and, pointing to a spot among the reeds at
the edge of the water, he uttered an exclamation of satisfaction.
"I thought as much," he said. "This is the spot where the
murder was committed. Look at this muddy earth, and this
broken reed. This is the work of a heavy man struggling in the
soft soil. But look here, too! Here are some little clear marks
of someone running away from the water. Here are the tracks of
many feet, but none of them are quite so clear as these. Now look
at this muddy boot-print. It is a very rare thing to find such a
large print. This is not a country in which people wear boots of
this size." He turned round to Lestrade and myself and smiled
triumphantly.  "Well, gentlemen," he said, "we have now solved
the case."

At the edge of the pool there was a steep bank, and Holmes,
descending this, went down on his knees and examined the mud
closely. Then he rose again, and, with a triumphant cry, pointed
to a particular spot among the reeds. "There is the place where
he stood," he exclaimed. "The assassin must have passed through
the reeds, for they are bent and broken, but there is no trace of
mud on his boots. Hence, it follows that the assassin must be a
man who did not approach the pool from the side of the path."

"But how about his boots?" I asked.

"The mud is soft and sticky, but this grass is dry. Hence it
follows that the assassin was a man who had come up to the
pool from the grass. That is clear, is it not?"

"Yes," said Lestrade. "But what then?"

"A man might come from Hatherley Farm across the meadows, or even
from Boscombe Hall, without going near the path," Holmes observed
"You are quite right."

At the edge of the pool there were some further indications—a
broken branch, and the remnants of what appeared to be a
recently extinguished cigar. Holmes picked up the cigar, examined
it with a curious smile, and then tossed it into his pocket.

"This is rather important," he remarked. "The ash is quite dry.
It must have been left sometime yesterday."

"What is the point?" I asked.

"The pool had been examined yesterday by the police," he
answered. "If the cigar had been there last night, it would
scarcely have been so dry as it is. It has been raining hard, you
see, and this would have damped it to some extent. If only it had
rained a little harder," he added, his face settling into the
characteristic mask of the Sherlock Holmes of Baker Street.

At the edge of the pool he spent some time examining the
ground, carefully measuring with his foot the distance between
various points. Then, with a somewhat heightened colour, he
returned to the path and continued his rapid walk along the
woods. At the spot where the murder had taken place we stopped
and made a very careful examination of the ground.

"This is where the blow fell," said Holmes, pointing to a patch
of grass which was more worn than the rest. "The other marks are
the steps of the two McCarthys. My attention was first called to
the matter by young McCarthy's vague description of something
grey. It could not have been his own overcoat, for that was
deposited in the wood, quite far from the body. But the nature
of the marks revealed it to me at once. It was the overcoat of
the older man. The blood stains were just such as I should expect.
The man was left in his overcoat with his back towards his son.
The murderer must have rushed in from the rear. Now let us look
at the other side of the pool."

The Boscombe Pool, which is a little reed-girt sheet of water
some fifty yards across, is situated at the boundary between the
Hatherley Farm and the private park of the wealthy Mr. Turner.
Above the woods which lined it upon the farther side we could see
the red, jutting pinnacles which marked the site of the rich
landowner's dwelling. On the Hatherley side of the pool the woods
grew very thick, and there was a narrow belt of sodden grass
twenty paces across between the edge of the trees and the reeds
which lined the lake. Lestrade showed us the exact spot at which
the body had been found, and, indeed, so moist was the ground,
that I could plainly see the traces which had been left by the
fall of the stricken man. To Holmes, as I could see by his eager
face and peering eyes, very many other things were to be read
upon the trampled grass. He ran round, like a dog who is picking
up a scent, and then turned upon my companion.

"What did you go into the pool for?" he asked.

"I fished about with a rake. I thought there might be some weapon
or other trace. But how on earth--"

"Now, gentlemen," said he rising, "I think that we have seen
enough. It is only a question of searching the wood until we
find the other boot. I should be very much surprised if it is
not a size six. But it is very important that we should find
out if this gentleman has a left foot turned in, and whether
he wears a peculiar boot. On the other hand, is the old man really
as ill as all that? I rather fancy that he is making a little
mountain out of a molehill."

"I don't understand," said Lestrade.

"You will," said Holmes. "In the meantime, we have our work cut
out for us. The lady, you said?"

"Yes, Miss Turner."

"Good. We must get her into the affair before we finish."

"Now, gentlemen," said he rising, "I think that that completes
the case. I propose at once that we return to Ross, and I shall
then, with your assistance, endeavour to lay before the
magistrates such evidence as will procure the release of young
McCarthy. I think it would also be advisable to telegraph to Mr.
Turner, as his presence will be needed."

"Then you are convinced that this young man is innocent?"

"I am, perfectly convinced of it. The absence of any sign of
struggle shows that the victim was struck from behind. The
murderer must have been someone who had his confidence, and who
could strike him without any chance of being observed. The mystery
of the cry 'Cooee!' is also explained. That was not a cry of
pain, but was simply the sound, which could be heard in the
woods, for which McCarthy had arranged to signal that all was well."

"And the cloak?"

"And the cloak?" repeated Holmes, laughing. "Well, Watson, I am
now ready to lay before you one of the most singular cases which
ever I handled. You may remember that when we examined young
McCarthy I showed you that he had the same peculiarity in his
left boot as the man whose tracks we saw in the woods. I also
pointed out to you that the tracks in the meadow were those of a
man with an inward twist to his foot. These two points can only
be explained by the same person. Now young McCarthy has no such
twist, but we have already learnt that there is another young
man with a similar twist, who, in addition, had a singular
peculiarity about his left boot, which would have struck the
eye of an ordinary observer as being unusual."

"Who was he?"

"James McCarthy's friend, Mr. William Crowder, the gamekeeper."

"What about him?"

"He is the man who is wanted."

"But why should he do it?"

"I think you will admit that the game-keeper had a good deal to
gain by the death of McCarthy, as he was certainly the one who
would have had the lease of the farm."

"But how did he come by it?"

"I believe the following to be the sequence of events: McCarthy,
who is a man of somewhat rough and reckless character, but with
a liking for sport, came back to Hatherley Farm on Monday. He
had his appointment with some one at the pool, and it was
obvious to Holmes, from the tracks, that the individual was not
the son but the gamekeeper himself, for both their boots were
square-toed and had unusual points. The place was obviously
chosen because they knew the locality and because they had the
confidence of the murdered man. On Monday afternoon McCarthy went
down to the Boscombe Pool, and the man went down there to meet
him and had a very violent quarrel. It was obvious, from the
conversation heard by the little girl, that McCarthy spoke very
harshly to his son. When the latter left the scene the other
person suddenly dealt him a violent blow from behind, for that was
the only direction from which the blow could have come, killing
him instantly. The gamekeeper then ran off, dropping the cloak in
his haste. The son, hearing a cry, rushed down the lane. In his
haste he stopped and listened to see if the cry was made again.
The murderer, seeing that his victim's son had not been killed but
had returned, was alarmed, and rushed back to get the cloak. The
son then knelt beside the body, and the murderer then stood for
some time within a dozen yards of the son while the son was
occupied with the body and could not see the man. The murderer
then made his way away, and the son went to the lodge-keeper,
reporting the fact. The whole thing is so simple, and is one of
those occasional cases where the obvious is utterly misleading."

"But how about this 'rat'?" asked Lestrade.

"Exactly! The 'rat' is the clue which has enabled me to unravel
the mystery. There was a suggestion that the dead man had used
the phrase 'a rat' just before his death. The gamekeeper must
have done this deed for the sake of money, which had something to
do with the goldfields of Victoria. It might have been a
mining-claim. The gamekeeper must have been associated with
McCarthy there and must have had some claim upon him that
McCarthy would not recognise. This was a quarrel about it and
McCarthy said something about a rat.

"Well,
"Now, gentlemen," said he, rising and brushing the dead leaves
from his coat, "I think that we have added a few more facts to our
case. It remains now only to find the missing link. We shall
have to get to work and follow this trail, but we need to get
back to Ross first."

"Well, Watson," said he, rising at last, "what do you make of it?"

"I confess that I am completely bewildered," I answered. "There
are points which seem to indicate the guilt of young McCarthy,
and there are others which would rather point to his innocence.
If he is innocent, who else could have done it?"

"That is what we have to find out," said Holmes, "before we go
any further. First of all, let us consider this case of the
vanishing grey cloth which young McCarthy says that he saw upon
the ground, and which was gone when he returned. Was that
possible?"

"I think it would have been very difficult," I said, "considering
how swiftly he ran, to have had time to remove it."

"Exactly! But was it removed? Is there any other possible
explanation?"

"What do you suggest, then?"

"Now, Watson," said he, rising and brushing off his knees, "I
think that we have added another observation to those which were
made at the inquest. This small wood was evidently the scene of
the struggle, and the murderer has come this way. See how the
grass is all torn up? The man was running, and he was heavily
laden. That is obvious from the depth of the footprints. And
observe, this grass is very long, yet it has been pressed down
only in a few places, showing that he kept to certain paths. He
had no companion."

"It has been a case of considerable interest," he remarked,
returning to his natural manner. "I fancy that this grey house on
the right must be the lodge. I think that I will go in and have a
word with Moran, and perhaps write a little note. Having done
that, we may drive back to our luncheon. You may walk to the cab,
and I shall be with you presently."

It was about ten minutes before we regained our cab and drove
back into Ross, Holmes still carrying with him the stone which he
had picked up in the wood.

"This may interest you, Lestrade," he remarked, holding it out.
"The murder was done with it."

"I see no marks."

"There are none."

"How do you know, then?"

"The grass was growing under it. It had only lain there a few
days. There was no sign of a place whence it had been taken. It
corresponds with the injuries. There is no sign of any other
weapon."

"And the murderer?"

"I understand," said Lestrade thoughtfully. "I think that I have
already grasped the situation. Would you care to consider the
question of the 'Cooee'?"

"I think that I have already explained that too," said Holmes
with a smile. "The facts are really quite simple. The young man
had an appointment with his father, but his father did not
know that he was coming. His father, however, was expecting
someone else at the pool, and that someone else was the murderer.
The father's cry of 'Cooee!' was meant for him, and it was this
call, which the son heard, that brought him to the scene."

"Good heavens!" cried Lestrade, "it was certainly the most
natural explanation."

"Very good indeed," remarked Holmes. "The criminal was concealed
among the reeds and he had to do his work quickly, for he had an
appointment, which he might fail to keep. He beat the unfortunate
man down, and then he may have dropped the stone in his flight."

"But the grey cloth?" asked Lestrade.

"That was undoubtedly his cloak, which he had dropped in the
scuffle. He returned for it later. I observed his tracks."

"And the fact that the man was struck from behind?"

"That was, of course, because his back was turned at the moment
when the first blow fell. The murderer came up silently behind
him. You remember how thick the trees are. He had to do it
quickly before his expected companion arrived."

"But his companion--the appointment?"

"We shall find him, too, before very long. I think that I have
now given you all the facts."

"And you mean that we should look for a man of such and such
appearance?"

"Exactly!"

"I shall set to work to-night," said Lestrade.

"I wish you the best of luck."

"There is a man who answers your description. A tall, well-dressed
fellow."

"Indeed!"

"Mr. John Turner of Boscombe Manor."


"Well, it is certainly a very ingenious theory," said Lestrade,
"and I confess that I am very much puzzled by this absence of a
weapon, and by the fact that the murderer should have dropped his
cloak. But it all amounts to this: that you have an idea that
somebody who answers to this description is the guilty man. But
who is he?"

"Well, now, that is what we should have to consider," said
Holmes, smiling. "It is a little more than a guess. Who is the
person who has an interest in preventing a marriage between the
young people? Who is it who might be supposed to have been
walking in this direction and yet may have been hidden from the
view of these witnesses? Who is the tall, slim, left-handed man
with a limp who wears thick-soled shooting-boots and a grey
cloak, smokes an Indian cigar, uses a cigar-holder and a blunt
penknife?"

"Why, it's Mr. John Turner," cried Lestrade.

"Exactly!" said Holmes. "But I must have a clear idea of the
man's position before I act."

"Why not go to the Hall and arrest him?"

"We have no evidence. We are in a curious position. Suppose we
consider the other side of the question. If Turner is the
murderer, why did the son not give him away?"

"Because he could not give him away. The father had just killed
the man who had wronged him, and had fled."

We lunched at the Hereford Arms, and afterwards Holmes, who had
left his bag there, went out alone, Lestrade remaining with me.
It was only about three when he returned, his face beaming with
triumph.

"The evidence is all complete," said he. "It is a simple case, as
I said before, but I wish that you had been with me. You would
have enjoyed the way I turned that fellow's own weapons against
him."

"Who was he?" I asked eagerly.

"John Turner," said Holmes. "The owner of this Hatherley Farm."

"Turner?" I cried out in surprise. "The man who seems to have been
so kind to McCarthy?"

"Exactly! The very kindness that was so loudly proclaimed
constituted the strongest case against him. The game-keeper
evidently recognized him, but did not know that his disguise was so
perfect as to mask his identity. It was the sheer audacity of the
crime which prevented suspicion. It was the assumption of
immense kindness and generosity on the part of the culprit that
made the case so difficult."

"But the motive?"

"The motive, my dear Watson, is still lacking. I have just come
from a very painful scene, however. Old Turner is dead."


"And the motive?"

"There is a missing will. Old Mr. Turner made another will the
day before he died, leaving his property to his daughter. It was
his old friend McCarthy who would have benefited most by the old
will being maintained. Then there was the question of the son's
marriage. It was no affair of the father's; it was a secret of
the son's. The son did not want a marriage, but the father did,
that the son might have the position he wanted."

"But how about the 'Cooee'?" I asked, for this had been a real
puzzle to me.

"It was a simple enough matter, my dear Watson," said Holmes.
"The 'Cooee' was a double bluff.  The older McCarthy knew his son
was in Bristol. He arranged the rendezvous by using the signal,
knowing only he would respond, thus creating a false alibi for the
son. He then used the same signal before he met his end, to
confuse matters further."

"Excellent!" I cried.  "But how did he know the son would come
back?"

"But there is no such person," cried Lestrade in amazement. "I
have made inquiries all round, and there is no one answering to
that description."

"Oh! there is such a person, and he's going to answer for it
before long," said Holmes confidently. "I shall be much obliged
if you will give the matter your immediate attention. I leave it
entirely to you. Now, Watson, if you are ready, we shall call
upon our friend, Dr. Willows, and afterward take a stroll around
this charming countryside before we leave."

Lestrade shrugged his shoulders. "I am a practical man," he said,
"and I really cannot undertake to go about the country looking
for a left-handed gentleman with a game leg. I should become the
laughing-stock of Scotland Yard."

"All right," said Holmes quietly. "I have given you the chance.
Here are your lodgings. Good-bye. I shall drop you a line before
I leave."

"I think that I have got enough now to work upon," he remarked
at last. "It is a most singular case, and one which has
presented some most unusual features."

"You seem to have solved it to your own satisfaction," I
observed.

"Yes, it is perfectly clear to me. It may not be so clear to a
British jury, but I am confident that I shall get a verdict of
not guilty for James McCarthy."

"But who is the real culprit?"

"John Turner," said Holmes. "The man is a scoundrel."

"It's a most damnable business," he said at last, pushing his
plate away. "This poor Turner has lost his life through it, and
I am sure that the blow which has fallen upon him will be the
death of him. The fellow is evidently a scoundrel of the
deepest dye."

"But how could you guess that it was he?" I asked.

"Because it was impossible that it could be anyone else."

"I understand, but how did you get the clue?"

"From the facts, my dear Watson. From the facts."

"What facts?"

"Everything points to it. For example, the young man's story,
the incident of the 'Cooee,' the statement of the girl that her
father saw McCarthy and his son quarreling, the fact that the son
had his hands stained with blood, the dying allusion to a rat,
the grey cloth, the footprint, the game leg, and the missing
cloak. There is a little more to it than that, my dear Watson,
but it is enough, I think, to show you how it all fits together."

"What was there more?" I asked, eagerly.

"We will talk of that later. It is too late now. Let us drive
down to the station."

"That's a queer case, Watson," he remarked at last, more to
himself than to me. "What a fool a man is to get his heart
broken by a pretty face. That's what Turner is suffering from. He
has lost his nerve. He has been afraid to tell his story lest
people should blame him for having been so easily imposed upon.
He is a man of good instincts, but he is as easily led as a child.
He is now in a state of abject terror. He has told his story
already. It is I who must tell it to the world."

"What! Is Mr. John Turner the murderer?"

"He is."

"How can you prove it?"

"By the evidence of his own actions, and the corroboration of
all the circumstances. I have only to fit the evidence to the
man. It is quite a simple matter. But I must have your help
once more, Watson. You have a good deal of common sense, which
makes you such a good listener and such a patient friend. I will
write a note and you shall be my messenger."

"It's a most damnable business," he said at last, pushing his
plate away. "This man Turner is a hound, a fiend. I know it is
only circumstantial evidence, but I am morally certain that this
is the solution."


"It's a most damnable thing," he said, pushing his plate away.
"This man Turner is a hound, a fiend. His conduct is unpardonable.
To think that he should have been allowed to go free, and that
this young lad should have been arrested at all, is enough to
make one despair of justice."

"But surely you don't mean to say that there is any doubt of the
criminal?" I exclaimed.

"Not the slightest. We have only to lay our hands upon the man,
and we have him. The facts are all in his favour. But it is a
curious thing. A most curious thing."

"What is that?"

"Look here, Watson," he said when the cloth was cleared "just sit
down in this chair and let me preach to you for a little. I don't
know quite what to do, and I should value your advice. Light a
cigar and let me expound."

 "Pray do so."

"Well, obviously the 'Cooee!' was a prearranged signal between
father and son. But the son was not there. Therefore the 'Cooee!'
was meant for some other person. That other person must have been
the murderer, since only the murderer could have known that the
father was there."

"Well, obviously, the 'Cooee!' was a prearranged signal between
father and son. But the father could only have given the signal
after having seen his son. Therefore, the son must have been in
sight of his father before the 'Cooee!' was given. But the son
was not in sight of his father until he reached the edge of the
pool. Therefore, the father must have been either at the edge of
the pool or very near it when he gave the signal. Now, let us turn
to the other point—the dying reference to a rat."

"Well, obviously the 'Cooee!' was a prearranged signal. It was
given by the murdered man to someone whom he expected. It was
given before he saw his son, and therefore it could not have been
for him. Then it was given to warn someone that he had arrived,
and to bring that person down to Boscombe Pool."

"What an extraordinary deduction!"

"Simple, my dear fellow, simple. And now for the other clue--the
dying reference to a rat. What was the point upon which the two
men had quarrelled? Something concerning Miss Turner, said she.
Now, the elder man had, as we know, had the sole experience of
the gold-fields in Victoria. The son had spent his life in
England. The father could have told the son something that
referred to the gold-fields and which would have explained the
quarrel."

"Well, obviously the 'Cooee!' was a preconcerted signal between
father and son. That is what the coroner's jury seems to have
taken for granted; but it is a curious thing that a man should
cry out 'Cooee!' before he knew that the person whom he wished to
signal was within hearing. Why did the father cry out before he
knew that the son was there? It was because someone else was
listening who might convey the news. That 'Cooee!' was the
preconcerted signal between him and the third person. That third
person must have been someone who knew the signal and was
watching the two."

"Excellent!" I exclaimed.

"And what about the dying reference to a rat?"

"That also points to the same thing. A rat is a very familiar
and very elusive creature. It might convey the idea that the
third person was a man who was very hard to catch."

"And who was he?"

"John Turner," said Holmes.

"Well, obviously it could not have been a prearranged signal, for
the son was away in Bristol. It was a cry for help. Now who was
it who could possibly be in need of help? The son, the father, or
the murderer? It could not be the murderer, for he was clearly
the strongest of the three. Who then was it?"

"The father."

"Precisely. But what help could he need, and from whom could he
need it? I answer, that he needed help from his son, and that he
was in danger from the murderer. Now, if you are following me
carefully, you will see that the murderer must have known that
the father was going to be in such a danger, and must have
arranged to be in a place from which he could see his danger and
rush to his aid. The murder would occur only if the father's son
were not there to prevent it."

"But that is a very complex hypothesis," I said.

"It is, at any rate, well founded upon facts which are clearly
proved. Now, let us look at the other mysterious circumstance—
the dying man's exclamation about a rat. What does it point
to?"

"I don't understand."

"It points to a very obvious fact—that the murderer was a man
whose dress or appearance was very similar to that of his victim,
and that they were, therefore, indistinguishable. Hence the
dying man’s exclamation that he was attacked by a man like himself—
a ‘rat’ in the thieves' jargon."

"Well, obviously it could not have been meant for the son. The
son, as far as he knew, was in Bristol. It was mere chance that
he was within earshot. The 'Cooee!' was meant to attract the
attention of whoever it was that he had the appointment with. But
'Cooee' is a distinctly Australian cry, and one which is used
between Australians. There is a strong presumption that the
person whom McCarthy expected to meet him at Boscombe Pool was
someone who had been in Australia."

"What of the rat, then?"

"It is a rather singular coincidence, is it not? Here is our
Australian. He comes over to England, settles down in
Herefordshire, and takes Hatherley Farm. But he does not break
off his relations with his old associates in Australia, for we
find him always ready to give a 'Cooee!' to his friend of Ballarat
when he wishes to meet him. Now, let us consider this map again.
Ballarat is in Victoria, and we find there that a considerable
part of the country is covered with a network of small lakes
called 'Billabongs.' What is a billabong?"

"An Australian term for a waterhole," I answered.

"Precisely. Now look at the map and observe the position of these
'billabongs.' Do they not remind you of Boscombe Pool? Do you not
see the similarity? Boscombe is a billabong itself."

"It is a long shot, but it is the only one that I can see. Now
let us look at our other clue. What did young McCarthy see when
he ran back to his father, just before he went for help? Something
grey, he said, lying some dozen yards from the body, some dozen
yards from the edge of the wood. Now what might that be? A grey
cloak, he thought. So it may have been. But it may have been
something else. The man was left-handed and limped with his
right leg. A left-handed man would drop his cloak from his left
side. That would account for the position of the cloak. And now
you see the rest."

"It is only common sense after all," he answered, lighting a
cigarette.  "Now you see that the appointment was made for three.
The man arrived at the spot, and, finding that he had to wait,
walked up and down. There is an indication that he was very nervous
and restless, for his steps are much wider and more hurried at
first than at the end of the track. Then he saw his son approach,
and, evidently, so far from being pleased at the meeting, he tried
to avoid him. He turned and walked away. His son then called to
him. He turned again, and there was a quarrel. Then there was a
sudden and violent attack, and a struggle. The old man fell,
injured, his son kneeling beside him. The murderer then came
back and, seeing the son kneeling, was able to escape, leaving
behind him only his cloak, which the son never saw. The murderer
had, however, already reached the wood, for I found the square
boots which he wore close to the edge of it. These are facts,
Watson, facts which are quite independent of the vagaries of
your imagination. Now for the inference."

"It is at least suggestive. Now let us consider another point.
This man was very anxious that his son should marry Miss Turner.
Why? Because she was the heiress to a considerable fortune, and
because he hoped in that way to recover some of his lost wealth
which he had squandered in Australia. He knew that Turner would
not consent to the match, and he knew also that his own son was
not in a position to do so, for he is a young man with many
faults but with a very tender heart, and is much too honourable
to have taken advantage of his father's wishes by forcing his
daughter into a marriage. The father, however, was utterly
unscrupulous. What did he do? Did he take the only course which
would secure his aim? Did he commit this murder, and then,
supposing his own son to be the criminal, did he endeavour to
place him in such a position that his escape from justice would be
secured?"

"It seems most probable."

"It is obvious, and yet it may be that I have overlooked some
essential fact. We have ascertained, however, that the man's
father had made his money in Australia, and that he had spent
many years in Ballarat. It is a fair inference that the criminal
must have been there also. If you look at the map you will see
that a considerable distance separates the Boscombe Pool from the
residence of Mr. Turner. It is much more probable that the
appointment was made at some spot which was halfway between the
two. The place where the man was murdered was at the edge of Mr.
Turner's park, which is contiguous to the Boscombe Pool. The body
was found near the boundary line. The inference is clear."

"That the criminal lived near Mr. Turner," I suggested.

"Exactly."

"It was the gamekeeper, then?"

"Precisely so. His left foot showed a peculiar inward twist when
seen walking in the grass. The man limps. His boots are square
toed. The man wears shooting-boots. His height is about six foot.
The man is left-handed. The man's name is John Turner, and he is
the criminal."

"It is obvious. And now, you see, I had narrowed the field down
considerably. The possession of a grey garment was a third point
which, granting the son's statement to be correct, was a
certainty. We have come now out of mere vagueness to the definite
conception of an Australian from Ballarat with a grey cloak."

"Certainly."

"And one who was at home in the district, for the pool can only
be approached by the farm or by the estate, where strangers could
hardly wander."

"Quite so."

"Then comes our expedition of to-day. By an examination of the
ground I gained the trifling details which I gave to that
imbecile Lestrade, as to the personality of the criminal."

"But how did you gain them?"

"You know my method. It is founded upon the observation of
trifles."

"His height I know that you might roughly judge from the length
of his stride. His boots, too, might be told from their traces."

"Yes, they were peculiar boots."

"But his lameness?"

"The impression of his right foot was always less distinct than
his left. He put less weight upon it. Why? Because he limped--he
was lame."

"But his left-handedness."

"Excellent!" I exclaimed. "And the man?"

"The man was John Turner, of course. It was to him that
McCarthy had the appointment. He had learned from his daughter
that the younger man had a wife in Bristol, and was averse to
marrying his own daughter. He wanted to get McCarthy out of the
way so that his daughter would be free to marry him. He would
have got rid of the son, too, if he had thought it necessary."

"But how did you make certain of this?"

"How did I make certain? Well, in the first place, the gamekeeper
saw the son going towards the pool. The gamekeeper has just been
employed by Turner. The old man was very ill, and did not want
trouble or publicity. He sent his man, the gamekeeper, to see
that McCarthy was out of the way. The gamekeeper could swear he
was following his father. The gamekeeper knew nothing of the
son's visit to Bristol, and was unaware that McCarthy would be
accompanied by anyone. The old man was to kill his enemy and
escape himself in the ensuing confusion. The blow was struck, and
the son’s arrival prevented the murder from being perfectly
successful. The man, realizing his error, concealed his cloak in
the woods. It may have fallen off his shoulders. He carried it
away to prevent any indication. The affair was almost at an end,
when the son's arrival caused the murderer to fly. That was when he
dropped the stone."

"But the stone?"

"Oh, that was merely to verify my theory, which I found fully
borne out by what I have learned to-day. The nature of the wound
corresponds with this jagged stone which I found in the woods
near where the body was found."

"Wonderful!"

"Excellent!" I exclaimed. "And the man himself?"

"Well, there we had to get down to the real, hard reasoning. I
had already come to the conclusion that the man was someone who
had been in Australia and who had had some relations with both
McCarthy and Turner. It is only amongst such persons that we can
look for the man who is at once an enemy of both and yet a
friend of both."

"Good heavens, Holmes! Is it possible that you suspected Mr.
Turner?"

"My dear fellow, it was my first thought. It was the obvious
solution. An elderly man with a game leg, left-handed, who had
spent years in the Australian gold-mines. He had a motive, for
McCarthy had a son who might put an end to his hopes. In an
emotional moment he had struck the man down and fled. The cloak
was a proof of his position, the size of his stride was evidence
of his height. Then I had only to make sure of his hands and his
pen-knife. I went to his house, and there I found a left-handed
man, and a blunt pen-knife upon his dressing-table. All was
simple, like the solution of a mathematical problem. But there was
another incident which did not fit into the theory.

"And that was?"

"This." Holmes drew out a small paper packet from his pocket.
"This was the reason that I was so long in returning. I had to
go to the lodge to get this."

He opened the packet and displayed a number of very fine gold
dust.

"What is that?"

"Gold dust, Watson. It was a very small packet, but it was of
some value, and it was just such a packet as would tempt a man
to commit murder."


"And the cloak?"

"It was there beside the tree. He had dropped it when he ran away,
but he had come back to fetch it. That is why his footprints are
found both on the path and on the edge of the reeds."

"Wonderful!" I exclaimed. "And the man?"

"John Turner," said Holmes.

"But how could you tell that?"

"Because of his missing socks. He is a man of wealth and position,
and would not be likely to wear such coarse socks as were found
near the scene of the murder. The other man's were there in the
blood, but they were the ordinary type of sock worn by the
countryman. Turner would not wear those socks."

"It is a beautiful deduction, Holmes. And the motive?"

"Jealousy, of course. This McCarthy had a secret about Turner
which he could use to blackmail him. It's a common motive."

"Excellent!" I exclaimed. "And the cloak?"

"Yes, that was a more difficult question. But a very important one.
The man had returned to the scene of the crime to remove his cloak,
a grey one, for the son had noticed that something grey was lying
there. That is what the lad had seen. The man was at the pool,
or on the pathway leading to it, at the very moment that the son
was there. But before the son got back, the man had vanished,
having taken his cloak with him. How was that possible? It could
only be possible if he had hidden himself behind some large
object. That is why I examined the beech tree. I found a
shallow cavity which had been filled with loose earth. It might
have been made in the course of some work, but there were other
traces of its use. I found traces of an Australian-made cloak, a
very peculiar kind of cloak, peculiar to Ballarat. I recognised
it from having seen several specimens of it in Australia. I then
examined the stone and I saw that it was stained with blood and
brain matter. I assumed that it was the murder weapon."

"It was a great feat!"

"Excellent!" I exclaimed. "And the cloak?"

"Yes, of course. There was mud upon the right sleeve and the
right skirt of the coat where it had brushed against the hedge as
he had come running away. We could not find the cloak, but there
was the evidence upon the hedge. The height of the man we gained
from the length of his stride, his weight from the depth of his
impression in the mud. You see it all now?"

"I have only one question," I said.  "Who was the man?"

"Holmes," I said, "you have drawn a net round this man from which
he cannot escape, and you have saved an innocent human life as
truly as if you had cut the cord which was hanging him. I see the
direction in which all this points. The culprit is--"

"Mr. John Turner," cried the hotel waiter, opening the door of
our sitting-room, and ushering in a visitor.

"I cannot imagine how you know it," said Turner, his voice harsh
and rasping. "You must have followed me."

"Only in thought," said Holmes. "I knew that you came to England
three years ago, and bought this house. I knew that you had
quarrelled with your neighbour, McCarthy, about a mining claim
back in Victoria. I knew that you had gone out to the pool
on the day of the murder."

"How can you possibly know all this?" asked Turner, his face
growing more and more ghastly.

"Because I have spent the last week in verifying every step
of your movements since you came to England. If you wish to know
anything else, I will tell you it, too. I will tell you that I
know also that your own son is in Melbourne and that he is well
and happy. What do you think of that as a little exercise in
deductive reasoning?"

The old man sank his face into his hands. "It was not my fault,"
he cried. "God knows it was not my fault! I would have given my
life to save him."

"Your life?" said Holmes gently.

"Yes, my life. I would give it now to undo what I have done. But
it is too late, too late!" He put his hands to his face, and his
whole body shook with his emotion.

"I wish to know nothing of your feelings," said Holmes coldly.
"What I desire is to know what happened at Boscombe Pool."

"It was a quarrel," said the old man. "He knew I had the money
and he was mad with greed."

"And your daughter?"

"She is innocent. She knew nothing."

"Tell me everything," said Holmes. "Tell me about Ballarat."

The old man sank back on the sofa, and he covered his face with
his hands. "What does it matter?" he cried in a voice which was
both acute and weak. "Let them know it all. It can make no
difference now. He is dead, and I cannot bring him back. I am
old and weary, and I could face the worst with equanimity, but
what I fear is lest this young man, James McCarthy, should have to
suffer for my sin."

"No," said Holmes. "Nothing can ever touch him. The case against
him has been broken up by my own investigations. It is I who am
your accuser."

"You?"

"Yes, I am the only witness of your crime."

"Then you may as well hear my confession. I have nothing to
hope for. He is dead. What matters it whether I am alive or
dead?"

"I shall certainly tell the truth. I shall make it known that
you did what you did not intend to do, and that you have already
paid the penalty."

"All?" The articulation was almost painful in its difficulty.  "Then
you know about Ballarat?"

"Yes, and about the attempted blackmail. You were at the diggings
with McCarthy, and you knew that he had made a fortune out of a
speculation in which you had also been concerned. You tried to
get him to come in with you, but he would not consent. Then you
wrote to him that you would expose him unless he handed over half
the profits of the speculation. You had an appointment to meet him
at Boscombe Pool, but you found out that he meant to take the law
into his own hands and ruin you instead. In self-defence you did
what you did."

"It was not planned," the old man groaned. "I swear it was not
planned."

"But it was done?" Holmes' voice was quiet, yet compelling.


"All?" The deep voice was hardly audible. "It is impossible."

"Oh, no, it is not impossible. You have been indiscreet, you see,
and I have been very observant. You have had two lives, Mr.
John Turner, and in the one you were known as John Turner, and in
the other, as Jack Stapleton. Now, do not let me frighten you,
but I believe that you are very near the end of your career."

"You know me, then?"

"Yes, I know you. You were a member of the Ballarat Reform Club in
Victoria, and a prominent figure, although somewhat too hot-headed,
in the local politics. I have also reason to believe that you
were acquainted with McCarthy, and that the affair had some
connection with the mysterious disappearance of a quantity of
gold."

"I have already explained to the police that I was in no way
concerned in the matter."

"Oh, yes, you did. That is rather a weak point in your defence,
however. A man who, only a few minutes ago, was almost crying out
for death does not usually find the strength to concoct a very
elaborate series of false statements. But let me give you a last
chance. Tell me how it was done, and I promise you that you will
have a far more merciful sentence than if you continue to evade
and lie to me."

The man sat up in his chair, his face in his hands. Then he
dropped his face into his hands again.

"If I tell you," he cried at last, "they will hang me as surely
as if I did the deed."

"You have already been condemned to death. Tell me how it was,
and perhaps I can help you."

The man gave a deep sigh.

"I will," he said.

The old man sank his face in his hands. "God help me!" he cried.
"But I would not have let the young man come to harm. I give you
my word that I would have spoken out if it went against him at
the Assizes."

"I am glad to hear you say so," said Holmes gravely.

"I would have spoken now had it not been for my dear girl. It
would break her heart--it will break her heart when she hears
that I am arrested."

"It may not come to that," said Holmes.

"What?"

"I am no official agent. I understand that it was your daughter
who required my presence here, and I am acting in her interests.
Young McCarthy must be got off, however."

"I am a dying man," said old Turner. "I have had diabetes for
years. My doctor says it is a question whether I shall live a
month. Yet I would rather die under my own roof than in a gaol."

Old Turner nodded, and then, in a low, broken voice, he gave us
the following account of the tragedy:  He had known McCarthy in
Australia, and had been, as Lestrade had said, a great benefactor
to him. McCarthy had subsequently become his tenant, but had
fallen into arrears with his rent, and Turner had threatened
him with eviction.  They had recently met, however, and had
agreed to let the matter stand over, Turner feeling some pity
for his old friend, and having some consideration for the fact
that his daughter's marriage to James McCarthy would settle the
matter without any dispute.

Old Turner nodded, and then, in a voice which was sometimes
broken by the agony of his disease, he gave us the following
account of the events which had led up to the terrible crime: "I
was formerly a miner in Victoria," said he. "I made my money
there, and returned to England a wealthy man. McCarthy was a
fellow-miner. I had known him well. We were partners for some
years, and I had every reason to believe that he was honest and
straightforward. I brought him back with me to England, and he
was my tenant and my friend. I was always a kind friend to him,
for I knew he was a man who had many points about him which were
not desirable. But his son was a fine lad, and I was fond of
him, and glad to think of his marrying my Ada." He paused for a
moment, and then continued in a low voice: "Three years ago I was
brought into touch with a gang of bushrangers, the most notorious
in the colony, and among them was this man McCarthy. I was out
alone one day and was met by three of them, armed. One I knew, but
the others were strangers. McCarthy ordered me to stand and deliver,
and I had to give up my purse. I tried to get help, but they
threatened me. One day I saw McCarthy in Ballarat. He was
wearing a coat which was familiar to me, but I did not think it
was mine, until I saw the gold buttons which I had had placed
there."

Old Turner looked from one to the other of us with an air of
desperate resolution. "I'll tell you everything," he said.  "It
began in the gold-fields of Victoria.  I was a young man then,
and he was a still younger one.  We were partners, and we made our
fortunes together.  He was a wild fellow, even in those days, but
I was always steady.  We were very close until--until a woman
came between us."

Old Turner nodded, and then, in a low voice, and with many
hesitations and repetitions, he gave us the following account of
the tragedy:  He had known McCarthy in Victoria, and had
always been friendly toward him.  McCarthy had, however, a
secret which would have ruined him and caused him to lose his
position and his fortune had it become known.  This secret was in
Turner's possession, and it was his fear that McCarthy would
reveal it, which caused him such great anxiety.

Old Turner nodded, and then in a low voice he gave a very clear
account of the whole tragic story. He had been in Australia
twenty years before, and had made his fortune there. He had
returned to England a couple of years ago and had taken Hatherley
Farm, where he had become intimate with McCarthy, who was also an
Australian. The two men had been friends, but there had been a
mistake and a quarrel. It appeared that McCarthy had been
engaged to a girl in Australia before he left, and that he had
also been guilty of some dishonesty in the business of the gold
mines. Turner had helped him and had kept his secret for years,
but the two had quarrelled, and Turner had discovered that the
man had not only broken his engagement but had also done him some
injury in his business dealings. He had found him at Boscombe Pool
and had had a violent scene with him. It culminated in a blow
from the heavy stone, which had felled McCarthy.

"It's as well," said the old man; "it's a question whether I
shall live to the Assizes, so it matters little to me, but I
should wish to spare Alice the shock. And now I will make the
thing clear to you; it has been a long time in the acting, but
will not take me long to tell.

"I was a young man, full of ambition, with a fine practice. I
had a place near Ballarat, and I was doing well, when this man
came to me. He was already in trouble, for he had gone out of
his way to get into a quarrel with an old digger. It was the
old, old story. There had been some dispute about mining rights,
and McCarthy had shot the digger dead. There was nothing to prove
him guilty but the weapon in his hand when he was taken. A clever
man would get him off, I said to myself. I had read in the
papers about my success in defending men accused of similar
crimes, and I was not mistaken. I took the case. It was a
singular one. I did get him off. I should never have done so had
it not been for the extraordinary coincidence that the dead man's
brother was at that moment dying in the hospital, so that the
only witness to the occurrence was removed. But it proved a fatal
case for me. The villain held it over my head, and made me his
tool.

"I was a young man then, fresh out from England, and I was
looking for gold. I was in Ballarat, and I met him there. He was
a handsome, dashing fellow, but he was a wicked one, too. I was
very keen on making money, and I was not too nice about the way I
got it. I put my whole life into it. That man, McCarthy, was a
schemer, a very clever schemer. He got hold of me when I was doing
something not too straight, and threatened to expose me, and
thus ruined my chances in the business. He demanded money, more
money and still more money from me for a long time. But the end
came when I brought my money back to England and set up for
myself. He was still following me, and, when he found I would not
give him any more money, threatened to give me away. I said to him
that I would do him a mischief if he did anything of the sort.
And that is what I did."

"I was a younger man then, a medical student, full of energy and
hope, but with very little money. I came across him at Ballarat
on the way over. He was a wild, reckless fellow, heavily in debt
and with no particular reputation. But he had one thing: he knew
where to find gold. He had shown me several places in the
neighbourhood, and I had made a considerable amount of money. We
came home together and were fairly intimate. I had a young
sister. She was engaged to be married, and this man, McCarthy,
began to persecute her in every way that he could--following
her about, writing her letters, even threatening her openly in
the street. She was afraid of him. I told him that if he didn't
leave her alone, I would make him suffer. I kept to my word, and
he assaulted me and I was knocked down. I had to fly from the
country. He used his influence to get me convicted and
imprisoned. That was the first time I had ever known what it
meant to be in his power.

"I was in Victoria then, and made my money at the gold-fields.
I was young, a strong, hearty man, and I wanted a wife. I fell
in love with a young woman, the daughter of a neighbouring
digger, and we were to be married on a certain day. I went out
to Ballarat to buy some things for her, and when I came back I
found my sweetheart was gone. McCarthy had her in his hands. He
had poisoned her mind against me, and had used his influence to
persuade her that I was a dangerous man. She would not hear a word
that I said, and would not leave his company. She died within a
year, and left McCarthy her fortune; and that was the end of that.

"I was a young man then, fresh from home, and I fell in with
McCarthy in the colonies. He was a man of great charm and
influence, but beneath it all he was a monster of vice. He had
some hold over me, and for years I was his tool and his accomplice.
We were in a big gold claim at Ballarat. I was a pretty good
prospector, and I struck it rich. We had our shares, but he,
through his influence and charm, got the biggest part. Then he
began to blackmail me. He had some dreadful secret about me, which
he said he would expose unless I agreed to do whatever he
wished."

"It was in the early '60's at the diggings. I was a young chap
then, hot-blooded and reckless, ready to turn my hand at
anything; I got among bad companions, took to drink, had no luck
with my claim, took to the bush, and in a word became what you
would call over here a highway robber. There were six of us, and
we had a wild, free life of it, sticking up a station from time
to time, or stopping the wagons on the road to the diggings.
Black Jack of Ballarat was the name I went under, and our party
is still remembered in the colony as the Ballarat Gang.

"He knew me at once. It appears that he had followed me from
Australia. The devilish cunning of the man is past all belief. He
had tracked me across half the world with the single idea of
revenge in his heart. He would wait for years, if necessary, to
get the chance. I saw his eyes, and I knew the dreadful fate
that awaited me. He threatened to reveal all if I refused to pay
him a large sum of money. He claimed I had killed his father.
I never did. His father had been killed in a drunken brawl.
However, it was true that I and my gang had been involved in the
killing of four troopers, and he was not far from the truth when
he said it was my gun that killed his father. It was my gun.
 I had no choice but to agree. Since then I have lived in fear,
and I have been paying him sums of money at intervals. He was
clever enough to find out where I lived. He had to be paid regularly.
He followed me about like a hound. He came to my house, and even
proposed a marriage between my Alice and his son James. It was
an awful scheme, and he meant to rob me to the end.

"I was to give him a large sum of money and he would not reveal
my past. Otherwise, he would inform against me.

"Well, last Monday, he came down and tried to get more money from
me. I went down to the pool with the intention of getting rid of
him. We met, and it all came out. I was in an awful rage. I struck
him, but I didn't mean to kill him." He paused for some time, while
he wiped his brow with a handkerchief.


"He seemed to know me at once, and he began to bluster, to
threaten, to make hints about the Ballarat business. I tried to
reason with him, and to explain that I was an altered man, but he
was brutal and violent, and laughed at my repentance. 'If you
want to keep out of trouble,' said he, 'you'll do what I tell you.
I have got you in my power, and I can ruin you if I choose.'

"He knew me at once--it was not likely that I should forget his
face. 'John Turner,' said he, 'you can't forget me. I am the man
whose life you saved at Ballarat.' I didn't deny it. 'Well,' said
he, 'you have done very well out of it, eh? Now it's my turn. You
have been a rich man for twenty years. I have been a poor one for
twenty years. I am going to have my share.' He came straight to
the point. It was a cool, clear business proposition. He said
that he would not molest me if I made him a present of two
thousand pounds. Otherwise, he would come out into the country
here and expose my criminal past to my neighbours and my
daughter. He said he would ruin me if I did not pay him the money.

"He knew me at once. It seems that he had been watching me for
days. 'John Turner,' said he, 'you may think yourself safe, but
you are not. I have followed you from Ballarat. I am not a man to
be trifled with. I have paid you many attentions. I am your
debtor, but the only debt which I owe you is that I am going to
kill you as you killed my mate twenty years ago. I have not
forgotten the way you looked at me as I lay there with my head
against the wheel. That little touch would not escape a man like
you who has always been quick to observe his foes.' That was how
he put it.

"He would not take my money. He never would. He lived on me, kept
me in his power, and made my life hell. The money which I gave
him was always spent on drink and bad company. He knew my secret,
and he knew that I dared not breathe it to a soul. The fact that
he held this over me gave him absolute power over me. I knew that
if I spoke out he could at any time have me arrested and sent to
the gallows. He used to say that I was a man who could never do
anything to save his life. It was at his last visit that I learned
that he was thinking of marrying my Alice. It was that that drove
me mad. I was ready to do anything to prevent such a calamity.

"I had a meeting with him at Boscombe Pool on Monday afternoon, and
I took the stone which I had already had in my pocket to give it
to him. I waited for him at the edge of the woods, and when he
came, and I heard him call out 'Cooee!' I dropped down behind the
great beech-tree and waited for him. I always carry a pocket-knife
with a blunt blade for cutting tobacco. I never was a man to be
impulsive, yet when he came and walked up to me, and I asked him
why he wanted my girl, and he laughed in my face, then I did it.
I hit him with that stone and struck him as hard as I could.
When I saw him fall down I ran away, and, seeing the grey cloak
which I had worn upon my way down, I took it up and carried it
away with me.


"He had tracked me down, the villain, and he held me in his power.
He had not forgotten my face. He knew my name, for I had used it
in my dealings with the colonial banks. He was in dire need of
money, and he came to blackmail me. For years, years, I have been
in his power. I have paid him sums of money that would make you
stare and gasp. I would have paid him all I possessed sooner than
expose myself to the scandal and the ruin. Had it not been for my
daughter I should have been ruined long ago. It is only a year ago
that I learned how he had come to England. He followed me from
the colonies. It may help you in the case. You can search out
the Ballarat records, and you will find that it was on the date
that I have given--June 3rd, 1863--that McCarthy was driving a
waggon and was attacked by six highwaymen, one of whom he swore
that he would bring to justice."

"And your appointment with him yesterday?" asked Holmes.

"It was a matter of business," said the old man, "a payment of
money."

"I believe you," said Holmes.


"'Here we are, Jack,' says he, touching me on the arm; 'we'll be
as good as a family to you. There's two of us, me and my son, and
you can have the keeping of us. If you don't--it's a fine,
law-abiding country is England, and there's always a policeman
within hail.'

"He meant to marry her to his son, James. That I would not stand.
I had always kept it from my girl, but I should have had to tell
her the truth, which would have broken her heart. Then he said he
would tell her if I didn't give my consent. I gave him every
chance, tried every means to get rid of him, but there was nothing
short of murder which would remove him. If only I had not spared
his life in the gold-convoy I should have had peace. But I had
gone too far; I was in his power, and he held me there."


"He said he would marry her, that she would be a suitable wife
for his son. The lad was a decent, well-meaning young fellow, but
I knew the old man's influence. I knew that he would force her to
marry his son in spite of herself, and I knew also that if she did
so it would break her heart. I would have done anything, anything
to prevent this, so I decided upon a desperate course. I thought
that if he was out of my way and his son was gone there would be
no one else left to threaten me. I saw him coming down to the
pool, as usual, and I followed him. I hit him from behind with a
stone which I had picked up from the road. I struck him but once,
and when he fell I made off with my cloak, fearing that it might
reveal me. Young McCarthy found his father and raised the alarm.
It was only when he had raised the alarm that I could dare to
return and take away the cloak. I did not want to leave it there.
It was all done as quickly as I could do it. The young man saw me
as I ran, but as I had never met him before he could not tell who
I was."

"His son, this lad, was a decent lad, and loved her like a brother.
But the father was like the devil. He had got his grip on me, and
I could not break away. I had to do it, to save my girl from
this man. So he and I had been walking that afternoon along the
path by the Boscombe Pool, and I had told him I would do it at
once.

"I had my revolver in my pocket, and, suddenly, I pulled it out
and fired. He fell before I knew where I was. I would have shot
him and got it over and done with if there had been no one else
there, but I was afraid of the young fellow. I was mad and
desperate, but I did not wish to hurt him.

"He knew that I would sooner kill him than let him have her. I
had refused him, and I had told him that he must leave me alone
and not trouble my life any more, but he was not to be moved. He
said he would do away with himself if I refused him. I was beside
myself with rage and despair. The thought came to me that if he
were dead my girl might be saved. It may be madness, but I swear
to you that it was mercy which drove me.

"He knew that I would sooner kill him than consent to that. But
he also knew that my life hung on a thread, and that if I raised
a hand against him my whole past would come out. So he went on
driving me to despair until I did consent--if he would leave me
and go back to Australia. It was at Boscombe Pool that we met. I
had money to give him, and when he came to take it I had planned
to kill him. I hit him and threw him into the pool. I intended to
let it look like an accident; and it would have been an accident
if it had not been for his son, the lad. He must have been
following his father. I heard him, and I caught a sight of him. He
came rushing forward and caught me, with his back towards me, in
the act of killing his father. That was the moment that I
dropped my stone and picked up his coat. I was mad with
terror. I saw the lad's eyes fixed upon me. In a moment I had
caught his coat and run."

"His son, you see, had grown up, and so had my girl, and as I was
known to be in weak health, it seemed a fine stroke to him that
his lad should step into the whole property. But there I was
firm. I would not have his cursed stock mixed with mine; not that
I had any dislike to the lad, but his blood was in him, and that
was enough. I stood firm. McCarthy threatened. I braved him to do
his worst. We were to meet at the pool midway between our houses
to talk it over.

"In view of your health and the great services which you have
done to the country in the past, I shall inform the authorities
that you are a very sick man, and I shall endeavor to have the
case settled as quietly as possible. There will be some
scandal, I am afraid, but I shall do my best to minimise it."

"God bless you, Mr. Holmes," said the old man solemnly. "May your
life be as happy as you have made mine."

"I shall keep your confession, of course, but I shall not use it
unless it is absolutely necessary. I shall take steps at once to
let young McCarthy know of the truth, and I have no doubt that
with this information we shall be able to clear him. The case
will then be in the hands of the proper authorities, and if you
are arrested you will have the chance of explaining your conduct
to the court."

"I shall go to young McCarthy, and I shall say to him, 'My dear
fellow, I have found out all about your father. I am satisfied
that you had nothing to do with his death. Your father was a very
wicked man, and he had an enemy in John Turner of the Hall. This
enemy tracked him down and struck him dead. It is probable that
he will never be brought to justice, but, at least, you will not
have to suffer.'"

"I shall use this confession to save young McCarthy. I shall
then hand it over to the authorities, and let them deal with it
as they think best. It is, I admit, a very terrible and a very
complicated situation, but I see no other way out of it. The
confession must be made, and when once it is made I trust that the
circumstances will help us to secure the best possible
settlement."

"I shall take this statement to the authorities and let them
deal with it as they think best. I shall also give them such
information as I have acquired concerning the criminal, and
shall leave them to unravel the remainder of the matter. Meanwhile
I shall go back to London by this evening's train."

"And young McCarthy?"

"He will be released, I hope, to-morrow."

"I thank you for what you have done for me," said the old man,
his eyes shining with gratitude. "I might have swung for it all."

"It was a singular case with some very unusual features,"
remarked Holmes as we drove back to the station.

"In view of your health, nothing. You are yourself aware that you
will soon have to answer for your deed at a higher court than the
Assizes. I will keep your confession, and if McCarthy is
condemned I shall be forced to use it. If not, it shall never be
seen by mortal eye; and your secret, whether you be alive or
dead, shall be safe with us."

We did not see him again.  A week later, we received a telegram
from Lestrade stating that Turner had died during the night.  Young
McCarthy, cleared of all suspicion, inherited his father's farm,
though he never fully recovered from the shock.  Miss Turner,
eventually, married a man more worthy of her, one not burdened by
the sins of the past.
We waited for some time in silence. Then Holmes pushed back his
chair.  "Now, Watson, we must pack our bags.  The game is over, and
it is time for us to return to London."

We heard later that he had lived for several months and had
died peacefully in his sleep.  Young McCarthy was released, and
Miss Turner's happiness, when she learned the truth, was as
unbounded as her gratitude to Sherlock Holmes.  Lestrade, who
had been quite confounded by Holmes' analysis of the case,
eventually received his due credit for the part he had played.  His
official report showed, of course, that the evidence against
young McCarthy was entirely circumstantial, but added, in justice
to the detective, that it was an exceedingly ingenious case.

Holmes refolded the confession and placed it in his pocket.  "Well,
Watson," he said, turning to me, "that was a near thing.  Young
McCarthy is safe, and the real villain has been unmasked."


We drove to the station, and Holmes was silent until we had passed
the junction and were nearing London. Then he said:  "That was a
remarkable case, Watson.  The motive was sufficiently singular.  I
am not sure that the methods of the criminal were not as remarkable
as the motive itself."

"God help us!" said Holmes after a long silence. "Why does fate
play such tricks with poor, helpless worms? I never hear of such
a case as this that I do not think of Baxter's words, and say,
'There, but for the grace of God, goes Sherlock Holmes.'"
